Stocks fell in the second-slowest session of the year Monday as a spurt in long-term interest rates to the 7 percent level lured investors to the bond market.
The dollar fell against the yen on selling ahead of a key Japanese economic report but edged higher against other major currencies.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 28.85 points to close at 5,693.89. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,331 to 869 on the New York Stock Exchange, where volume of 281.4 million shares edged past July 29's 281.3 million, the slowest full session so far this year.
"The bond market is really the story of the stock market," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.

"As rates go up, stocks are looking more and more expensive," he said. "The whole mindset of bonds has changed 180 degrees in the past week. There are fears of higher rates and that the Fed will raise rates sooner or later."
In the bond market, the closely watched 30-year Treasury fell another 18/32 after tumbling 1-3/32 points on Friday, sending its yield up to 7 percent from 6.95 percent at Friday's close.
The last time the bond yield closed above 7 percent was July 30.
Inflation-sensitive bond yields shot up Friday to three-week highs as July durable goods orders rose 1.6 percent, against expectations of a 0.3 percent rise.

Analysts said bond prices were further weighed down in thin trading by upcoming bond offerings. The Treasury will sell $18.75 billion two-year notes on Tuesday and $12.5 billion five-year notes on Wednesday.
"August tends to be the lightest month of the year and the last week of August tends to be one of the lightest," said Phil Roth, Dean Witter Reynolds' chief technical analyst.
Metz said the flurry of merger pacts announced "was the only place with any real upside action, and Philip Morris."
Late Monday, the dollar fell to 107.65 Japanese yen from 108.15 yen late Friday. The dollar edged up to 1.4790 German marks from 1.4780 marks.
In commodity trading, coffee prices rose to their highest level in nearly a year on Monday and grains rose as worries about adequate supplies sparked speculator buying.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, September coffee rose 4.20 cents per pound and closed at 136.45 cents, its highest close since September 6, 1995.
Crude oil and product prices closed sharply lower, with gasoline prices hardest hit, with traders citing profit-taking after the recent run-up.
Crude oil for October delivery fell 34 cents to $21.62 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Overseas, the London stock market was closed for a public holiday. Tokyo's 225-Nikkei average tumbled 345.06 points, or 1.63 percent, to close at 20,883.74.
